newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FORECAST-Floods seen raising Cambodian inflation.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Floods seen raising Cambodian inflation.

text.p: Cambodia's inflation is expected to surge later this year due to flooding damage, government officials and analysts said on Thursday.

Flooding hit the country in late September and early October, claiming more than a dozen lives and leaving almost a half a million people facing food shortages. More than 200,000 hectares of rice fields were flooded.
Cambodian year-on-year inflation for September was 6.8 percent, while the monthly consumer price index was up 0.57 percent from August, the finance ministry said.
Those numbers will flare upward by late November, Sok Hach, economic adviser for the Finance Ministry, told Reuters.
"Based on our experiences with the 1994 flood, we expect to see the real impact by December, because the harvest will start and we will know exactly how much we lost," he said.
The government had been hoping to hold Cambodia's inflation rate, which has hovered at around seven percent in recent months, under 10 percent this year.
Kao Kim Hourn, chief of Cambodia Institute for Cooperation and Peace think tank, said the flood was hitting the economy at a bad time, when many infrastructure improvements were underway.
"It's very unfortunate for Cambodia...that we have to spend more money not building new things but rather repairing what we have," he said.
The floods will also cut gross domestic product (GDP) growth by one percent this year and cost $30 million in damages, Sok Hach, economic adviser for the Finance Ministry, told Reuters.
Cambodia's GDP growth was forecast at seven percent for the year, but will now be closer to six percent, Sok Hach said.
The country's GDP is among Asia's lowest, at under $300 per capita.
